assessment.nobel_worthiness: Nominal rigidities and the New Keynesian framework underpin the modern analysis of monetary policy. Staggered pricing and wage setting, interest-rate rules and the micro-founded policy framework have shaped central-bank practice and teaching worldwide. The field-wide influence is very large.
assessment.attribution: The list is crowded, so attribution has to be cut hard. Calvo (time-dependent pricing), Taylor (staggered contracts and the rule) and Woodford (the integrated micro-founded policy framework) are the clearest conceptual anchors. Gali, Gertler, Christiano, Eichenbaum and Smets are major contributors on the quantitative and empirical side, and are excluded only because of the three-name limit.
assessment.maturity: Mature. The core contributions date from 1979-2003 and have been tested through decades of policy use, including the inflation surge of 2021-23 and the zero lower bound episodes.
uncertainties: Attribution is contestable, because several important contributors would be left out (Rotemberg and Clarida-Gali-Gertler are not credited in this candidate).
Bernanke was recognised in 2022 for banking and crisis work, so the committee may see some thematic overlap with recent macro prizes.
Evidence on the empirical fit of Phillips-curve models is mixed.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The heterogeneous-firm trade framework changed how economists understand the gains from trade. It covers selection, exporter premia and reallocation, and it opened up a large body of empirical and quantitative work. It follows naturally from the new trade theory recognised in 2008.
assessment.attribution: Melitz (2003) is the central source. Helpman, with Melitz and Yeaple, is the most important companion through the extensive-margin and FDI-versus-exports work. Redding has contributed substantially, notably in quantitative and spatial extensions. Related firm-level empirical work, such as Bernard-Jensen and Eaton-Kortum, is outside this candidate and complicates credit.
assessment.maturity: Mature. The work is more than 20 years old, is widely replicated, and is embedded in the standard toolkit for trade and productivity.
uncertainties: Credit-sharing with the firm-level empirical trade literature, which this candidate does not list.
Helpman also appears in B007, so a combined recognition across both trade candidates is possible but outside this ballot.
Quantitative welfare implications are sensitive to modelling assumptions.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Kiyotaki-Moore (1997) is a foundational model of collateral constraints that amplify and propagate shocks through credit cycles. It is one of the main theoretical foundations of macro-financial analysis and has been central since the 2007-09 crisis.
assessment.attribution: The collateral-constraint mechanism is cleanly attributable to the pair. Gertler and Gilchrist developed the related financial-accelerator and empirical lines with Bernanke, who was recognised in 2022. Limiting the proposal to Kiyotaki and Moore gives a tight, defensible credit assignment.
assessment.maturity: Mature. Nearly three decades of influence, extensive extensions and continuing use in policy models such as macroprudential analysis.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2022 banking-crisis prize may make the committee reluctant to reward the same theme again.
Empirical identification of collateral channels is still debated.
Whether the committee would prefer including Gertler as a third laureate.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Structural estimation of demand with differentiated products and endogenous prices (BLP) made modern empirical industrial organisation possible. It underlies merger analysis, antitrust evaluation and the study of market power, and it is used well beyond IO. Dynamic industry models (Ericson-Pakes) add further depth.
assessment.attribution: Pakes is the central figure across both demand estimation and dynamic games. Berry and Levinsohn are co-authors of the BLP method. Bresnahan, Reiss, Benkard and Levin made important adjacent contributions that are not included in a three-name proposal.
assessment.maturity: Mature. The approach has been standard since the mid-1990s and is used daily in practice, with long-run evidence of value.
uncertainties: The list is broad (seven names), so there is real attribution ambiguity, especially for Bresnahan.
Industrial organisation was recognised recently (Tirole 2014), though on different topics.
Credibility debates around structural versus reduced-form approaches continue.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The task-based view of technology and the China-shock evidence changed how economists and policymakers think about labour demand, local labour-market adjustment and wage inequality. Both strands are important and have large policy relevance.
assessment.attribution: Autor is the common thread, through task-based work and the trade-shock papers with Dorn and Hanson. Hanson is the clearest trade-side counterpart. Dorn is a major co-author. L. Katz's role is more linked to the education-technology race than to this particular bundle, so credit is spread.
assessment.maturity: Fairly mature. The key papers date from 2003 to 2016 and have been widely replicated or extended, but the long-run interpretation (permanence of local effects, automation versus trade) is still being debated.
uncertainties: The 2024 prize (Acemoglu) addressed technology and institutions in part, so there is thematic proximity.
Some of the persistent-effects findings have been challenged in re-analyses.
Attribution is blurred between task-based theory (Acemoglu-Autor) and the empirical China-shock work.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The misallocation framework provides a quantitative way to link firm-level distortions to aggregate TFP and cross-country income gaps. It has redirected growth and development research toward allocative efficiency and gives a bridge between micro data and macro outcomes.
assessment.attribution: Hsieh-Klenow (2009) is the key paper, and the two are the natural pair. Restuccia-Rogerson (2008) is an independent parallel contribution, and Restuccia is credited here, so priority and credit could be argued either way. Choosing two names is a judgment about the most influential single contribution.
assessment.maturity: Moderately mature. About 15-17 years of influence, with extensive application. Measurement of misallocation remains contested, particularly with respect to measurement error and markups.
uncertainties: Parallel and earlier contributions (Restuccia-Rogerson, Banerjee-Duflo) complicate attribution.
Measurement sensitivity: some estimated TFP gains shrink under reasonable corrections.
The 2025 and 2024 prizes already covered growth and development themes.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Population-scale administrative data on intergenerational mobility created a new empirical basis for studying opportunity, local environments and neighbourhood effects. The work links well to public-economics and welfare questions, and its policy significance is high.
assessment.attribution: Chetty is the dominant intellectual and organisational force in the programme. Hendren is central to the neighbourhood-effects and causal place-based analysis. Friedman and L. Katz are important co-authors on specific components, so credit is shared across a large collaborative group.
assessment.maturity: Less mature than the other top candidates. The main results are from 2014-2022, and the long-run replication and policy-effect evidence is still accumulating. Some findings, such as the causal interpretation of place effects, are still under scrutiny.
uncertainties: Collaborative scale makes credit hard to assign.
Timing: the committee may prefer to wait for further replication and long-run follow-up.
Mobility measurement across countries has an earlier literature (Solon, Björklund-Jäntti, Corak) that sets precedent.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Rubinstein's alternating-offers bargaining model (1982) is a canonical result in game theory. It gives a strategic foundation for bargaining outcomes and underpins models in labour, trade, macroeconomics and industrial organisation. It also serves as the micro-foundation for many applied models of search and matching.
assessment.attribution: The core model is Rubinstein's, and Ståhl's earlier finite-horizon work is a precursor, though Ståhl is not credited here and is, to my understanding, deceased. Wolinsky (bargaining in markets, with Rubinstein) and Binmore (interpretation and the Nash-programme link) are important but secondary.
assessment.maturity: Very mature. More than 40 years of influence. The main weakness for this ranking is that game theory has been recognised several times, and the field-wide marginal impact is mostly through theory and teaching.
uncertainties: Whether an application-oriented committee would prefer a more empirically influential candidate.
The contribution is theoretical and canonical rather than recent, and the recognition may be seen as overdue or as less pressing.
Attribution to Rubinstein alone leaves out Wolinsky and Binmore, whose contributions are real.
